title: Khema answers the king
hookLine: King Pasenadi asks the nun Khema whether the Tathagata exists after death; she answers with the sand of the Ganges and the depth of the ocean, and later the Buddha answers the same (SN 44.1)

cards: A king on the road, with a night to fill. In the Samyutta Nikaya, King Pasenadi of Kosala is traveling between two cities and stops for the night at a small town.
He sends a man to find an ascetic or a brahmin worth talking to. The man finds none. Only the nun Khema, a disciple of the Buddha, whom people describe as wise, learned, and a brilliant speaker.
So the king goes to her, bows, sits to one side, and asks: when a fully awakened one dies, what happens to him? Does he exist after death?

teach.b: First, four questions, one answer. Does the Tathagata, the one thus gone, exist after death? That hasn't been declared by the Blessed One, great king, Khema says.
Then he doesn't exist? Not declared. Both?
Neither? Not declared, each time. The king, puzzled, asks why.
Second, the sand and the sea. Khema answers with a question.

teach.h: SAND IN THE GANGES, WATER IN THE SEA.
teach.b: Great king, do you have an accountant who could count the grains of sand in the Ganges? No. Could anyone measure the water in the great ocean?
No; it's deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom. Just so, Khema says. The awakened one has let go of the body, the feelings and the rest, all the things we'd use to measure him.
Freed from that reckoning, he is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom, like the ocean. Third, the second conversation. Later the king asks the Buddha himself the same four questions.
The Buddha gives the same answers and the same similes, and the king says it's wonderful how teacher and disciple agree, in meaning and in wording. Fourth, a teacher in her own right.
Khema claimed nothing of her own: not declared by the Blessed One, she said, each time.
She had understood it herself, so well that his words and hers matched.
And notice the sand. A few days ago Rahula held a handful each morning, wishing for advice. Khema holds a whole river's worth, and uses it to say: some things can't be counted.

how: Khema's conversation with King Pasenadi is studied in Theravada teaching on the undeclared questions, and is told as an example of a nun whose understanding matched the Buddha's own.

o: forbidden questions that bring bad karma
undeclared: questions the Buddha set aside
unknowable to anyone but the Buddha

games.q: Khema and the king: tap the pairs.
p: asks if the awakened one exists after death
not declared by the Blessed One

s: Khema told the king the awakened one simply ceases to exist
she said that, like the others, this had not been declared, and compared him to the ocean.
the Buddha later gave the king the same answer and the same similes
the king marveled that teacher and disciple agreed in meaning and in wording.
the king went to Khema because she was the only well-known teacher he knew
his man searched the town and found no ascetic or brahmin, only the nun Khema.

games.q: you're Khema. a king asks you whether the awakened one exists after death. what do you do?
o: ask whether anyone can count the sand of the Ganges.
send him to the Buddha instead.
games.why: she answers with a question: who could count the Ganges' sand or measure the ocean? the awakened one, freed from all reckoning, is deep and hard to fathom like the sea.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something without a title, a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend who simply understood, and recall one thing they said that turned out to be true.
Then let the big questions you carry stay unanswered for a minute, without counting or measuring them. Just breathe, deep and hard to fathom, like the ocean in Khema's answer.

wordCard.voice: Abyakata, undeclared. The questions the Buddha set aside, which Khema answered King Pasenadi the same way, with the simile of the ocean. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali abyakata: undeclared, the questions the Buddha set aside, like the one the king asked Khema.

carryVoice: Your line: the same answer. Not repeating him, but seeing the same thing. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 44.1 (Khema Sutta: Khema and King Pasenadi)
